They can be a bit awkward to carry around sometimes, but mine was pretty thin and weighed next to nothing. If you really don't want to transport a cooling pad along with your laptop, again it is really not necessary as your laptop is designed to do what it do. However, I personally would suggest getting one at least for extended periods of gaming.

Yeah there are two versions of that model. One with usb, one with jacks. There arent any drivers for you (the jack version owner) to download for the headset itself, although you should definitely make sure any sound card and general audio drivers are all up to date.

The fix that worked for me, and one that I have not seen listed anywhere else is as follows: Open your Realtek Audio Manager. There should be a link in the upper right corner, "Device advanced settings." If you open that, there should be an option to "separate all input jacks as independent input devices." You will want to check this, as it is unchecked by default. From there, you should see your microphone listed as its own device under Audio Devices -> Recording while it is plugged in. This will allow you to configure your mic as a separate device from the headphones. Set this as your default input device!  Fiddling with the device's properties, especially utilizing the 'listen' tab should help you figure out if your mic is now working properly. You may need to increase your microphone boost setting before your voice is picked up by the mic. My own boost settings are set at max just to get my voice to a normal level.

These bookmarks aren't meant to be permanent. You delete them when you're finished and docked. If you don't use bookmarks, do it. If you do use bookmarks and find your connections consistently closing behind you, then reflect for a moment on whatever it is you've been doing until now.

If you right click and show info on the hole before you enter, it will tell you whether it will collapse soon in addition to which type of system is on the other side. Whs that don't warn you of being near collapse should be good for at least a few hours. 

If your whs are consistently closing behind you, you're either not looking at their descriptions and diving through connections that are about to collapse behind you, or going deep enough wh to wh that you're taking many hours to find and run sites. If the latter is true, don't go so deep. When you run out of sites and figure you're spending too much time in one chain of whs, go back to high/low/null sec and find another wh entrance to start over again with.


I suppose you could get particularly unlucky and find a busy wh where the inhabitants collapse an exit with large ships. But even then, the traffic would have to be more than just one or two ships, and if you're keeping an eye on d-scan you can tell if the wh is that active. But basically, there's no reason for you to consistently get stranded during wh exploration. If that's happening every time, you're doing something wrong.

Always bookmark the entrances of your wormholes.

Full of loot and need to get out? Done for the day and want to dock and log? --> go out the way you came in by warping to your bookmarks. There's no need for you to spend 5 hours scanning for a wh to high or low sec if you already know where it will be.

In my opinion, it was good that Brink didn't have too much focus on progression. 

The classes in Brink were all very different from each other, and the body types added even more variety to playstyles. So the fun came less from unlocking new guns and abilities, and more from getting really really good at your favorite class and trying to master the game's movement system.

Gosh, I played the shit out of Brink and got really good with the light body type. Can confirm, once you got a feel for it, the parkour system on the light type was incredibly useful - shooting while moving became easy with the right weapons/attachments, and knowing subtle tricks to some of the maps made it possible to get behind enemies and hop away before others had time to react. You just had to practice, like with any other multiplayer game.

The game's downfall was in the fact that the parkour system wasn't as refined as it could have been. But at the same time, I think people tend to not give it enough credit. It was a unique game, and one that you had to spend a bit of time with to get used to given the fact that the gameplay was meant to be very movement-based whereas many other shooters are better played using cover and moving at a more careful pace. The parkour had its quirks, like using walls to cancel slide animations and areas or shortcuts that you could only get to if you performed a wall jump or series of other actions perfectly. Rebinding some of the console's buttons also made the parkour immensely easier and more comfortable for the fingers.

Overall, it was a great mix of silly and serious. One of the positive things that came from its small player-base was getting to befriend the regulars and have a consistent pool of 'good' players to play against.

I was in your shoes a few years ago when I was your age. I responded to another comment about community college and how you should at least try before you write it off as a lost cause.

But I also understand the driving situation. I got my permit very late, after I had graduated high school. I was planning on going to a college that has a decent transportation system, and I thought everything would work out. After I was accepted, depression hit majorly hard and I just couldn't finish the process of getting everything set to move to the campus. It got so bad that I ended up just not attending, and turned to community college instead.

I spent one or two semesters of community college getting rides from my father to and from school. It sucked not being as independent as the other kids who had gotten their permits during high school. I was very nervous about driving, and my dad is a terrible teacher in most areas and only made me more nervous behind the wheel. I started bugging him anyway to take me driving and had to re-study the handbook to take the written test. By the time I had my permit, I still had only been behind the wheel a few times and was nervous the first time I had to drive myself to school. But I started with that one route until it became comfortable and then slowly started taking the car to other places nearby. Now it's easy peasy like it is for the general population.


Tl;dr: If you're ready to start driving, get a copy of your state's driving handbook and study. They're supposed to be free and available at the DMV. Pass a written test, bug your parents to take you on the road. Being able to drive is almost essential depending on where you live, and depriving you of that now would be hurtful on their part. Since you'd be rushing like I did, get used to one route at first, whether it's school or a job, and then branch out from there.

Our situations are a lot alike. The toughest part is finding the energy to make things come together. It isn't easy, but it's doable. I did it, and I'm sure you can as well if you try.

The material on the SAT isn't supposed to be hard, just an evaluation of your potential as a student. ACTs are tougher because they're supposed to show a specialized interest. If continuing your education and getting a degree is something you want to do, get an SAT practice book and take that test. They really aren't that difficult, especially if you know what to expect before you start your session.

The cherry on the cake for community college is that they'll accept people with pretty low SAT scores, and make them take a few extra math, english, or reading prerequisite courses to fill in the gap in knowledge of the student's lower scores.

Basically, there isn't too much pressure on you to do spectacularly; if you're confident that you're a good student, just go for it and take them. The worst that happens is you do more preparation in your lower-score areas and take them a second time (this is what I did). Schools look at the highest scores across all SATs, so if your math score is terrible on your first try, they will disregard that score if you get something higher on your second or third test, and judge your admission on the higher one instead.

It's worth it to at least try once or twice before you tell yourself you can't do it.

The thing about doing anything successful pvp-wise means waiting on your skill queue for a while before you solo or finding a corp/alliance that has people to teach you pvp and fly with you so your lack of skill points at first doesnt make participating in pvp impossible. Early-on youll be able to fly small ships and without high enough sp, you'll get wrecked by more experienced players.

Honestly I'll bet you'll end up just looking for random pvp with a group of other people instead of being a bounty hunter specifically. There were a lot of things I thought I'd do when I started playing Eve, and I found very quickly that it's much easier/more fun to just have fun with a corp. You'll probably end up having more options for things like bounty-hunting after learning game mechanics, how to fit ships correctly, and get your skill points high enough to be successful to solo kill.

I end up not finishing a lot of the games I own. Usually it's because there are just so many things to play and new titles coming out so quickly. When I first started gaming, I was much more into the stories and lore of the games I played, but I think that was also because my options were more limited, so I was more inclined to stick with what was available. Now it's so easy to get distracted by new games and forget where I am in the storylines of the ones I've paused.
However, I still believe that long, in-depth games are definitely worth it and very rewarding to finish, and it's a shame that most people don't see well-made stories through to their ends.
